target_units.text: What has come to be is what will come to be, and what has been done is what will be done; there is nothing fresh beneath the sun.

rationale: The source's eye is never filled with seeing; the proverb likewise calls human eyes insatiable, supporting the shared observation about unfulfilled desire.

rationale: The imagined announcement of something new is answered by appeal to earlier ages, elaborating the preceding denial of anything fresh beneath the sun.

target_units.text: What has come to be is what will come to be, and what has been done is what will be done; there is nothing fresh beneath the sun.

rationale: The general disappearance of earlier generations from memory becomes the more particular claim that neither wise nor foolish people retain enduring remembrance.

target_units.text: The words of Ecclesiastes, son of David, king of Israel in Jerusalem.

rationale: God-given human distraction appears in both passages; the target adds that people cannot discover God's whole work despite their inquiry.

rationale: The sweeping judgment of works beneath the sun as futility and resolve of spirit returns after the speaker examines his own achievements.

target_units.text: Then I looked upon all my works that my hands had done and the toil with which I had labored to do them, and behold, everything was futility and resolve of spirit, with no surplus beneath the sun.

rationale: Both deny human power to put what is twisted in order; the later saying explicitly situates the difficulty within God's works.
source_text: What is twisted cannot be put in order, and what is lacking cannot be counted.

target_units.text: Consider God’s works, for who can put in order the one whom God has twisted?

rationale: The speaker claims wisdom surpassing earlier Jerusalem figures; God's promise to Solomon likewise describes a wise heart without a comparable predecessor or successor.
source_text: I spoke in my heart, saying: Behold, I became great and added wisdom beyond everyone who was in Jerusalem before me, and my heart saw much—wisdom and knowledge.

target_units.text: behold, I have done according to your word. Behold, I have given you a discerning and wise heart, so that no one like you has been before you, and no one like you shall arise after you.

rationale: Both describe deliberately seeking wisdom and knowledge; the later search extends the inquiry explicitly to an ungodly person's folly, continuing and broadening the opening experiment.
source_text: I set my heart to know wisdom and knowledge; I came to know comparisons and understanding, for this too is resolve of spirit.

target_units.text: I turned, I and my heart, to know, examine and seek wisdom and a reckoning, and to know an ungodly person’s folly, harshness and delirium.

rationale: Increasing knowledge increases pain in the source; the closing warning similarly recognizes bodily weariness from much study.
source_text: For in much wisdom is much knowledge, and whoever increases knowledge will increase pain.

target_units.text: My son, beware of making many books; there is no limit, and much study is weariness of the flesh.

rationale: The experiment with gladness proves futile; the later comparison of foolish laughter with crackling thorns likewise ends by declaring futility.
source_text: I said in my heart: Come now, I will test you with gladness; experience good. But behold, this too was futility.

target_units.text: for like the sound of thorns beneath a cauldron, so is the laughter of fools. This too is futility.

rationale: Calling laughter delirium anticipates the later preference for mourning and wise rebuke over the gladness, songs and laughter of fools.
source_text: Of laughter I said, “Delirium!” And to gladness, “What are you doing?”

target_units.text: The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, but the heart of fools is in the house of gladness.

rationale: The experiment asks what people should do during their numbered days; the target asks who knows what is good during those same limited days.
source_text: I examined in my heart how to draw my flesh toward wine—while my heart guided me with wisdom—and how to take hold of folly, until I might see what good human beings should do beneath the sun during the numbered days of their lives.

target_units.text: For who knows what is good for a person in life, during the numbered days of his life of futility? He has spent them in a shadow. Who will tell a person what will be after him beneath the sun?

rationale: The source lists building houses among royal projects; the Kings unit explicitly includes the king's house and extensive building undertakings.
source_text: I enlarged my work; I built houses for myself and planted vineyards for myself,

rationale: The source's acquired slaves belong to its account of royal possessions; Kings distinguishes subjected peoples and Israelites' royal service, supplying a concrete parallel for organized royal labor.

target_units.text: any of the people remaining from the Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Canaanites, Hivites, Jebusites, and Girgashites, who were not of the sons of Israel—their children remaining after them in the land, whom the sons of Israel had been unable to destroy. rationale: The source accumulates silver, gold and riches of kings and regions; Kings records Solomon's gold receipts and tribute from regional kings and officials.
source_text: I also gathered silver and gold for myself, and the riches of kings and regions. I provided male and female singers for myself, and human delights—a male cupbearer and female cupbearers.

target_units.text: The weight of gold coming to Solomon in one year was six hundred sixty-six talents of gold,
besides the tribute of the subject peoples, the merchants, all the kings of the region beyond, and the satraps of the land.

rationale: The speaker combines surpassing greatness with retained wisdom; Kings likewise combines Solomon's surpassing wealth with surpassing discernment.
source_text: I grew great and surpassed everyone who was before me in Jerusalem; my wisdom also remained with me.

target_units.text: Solomon surpassed all the kings of the earth in wealth and discernment.

rationale: Joy in the speaker's toil is called his portion; the target likewise locates a person's portion in rejoicing in his works.
source_text: Whatever my eyes asked for, I did not withhold from them. I did not keep my heart from any gladness, for my heart rejoiced in all my toil, and this was my portion from all my toil.

target_units.text: I saw that there is no good except for a person to rejoice in his works, for that is his portion. For who will bring him to see what may happen after him?

rationale: The source finds no surplus in its completed works; Paul, after discussing resurrection, assures believers that their labor in the Lord is not empty.
source_text: Then I looked upon all my works that my hands had done and the toil with which I had labored to do them, and behold, everything was futility and resolve of spirit, with no surplus beneath the sun.

target_units.text: Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the Lord’s work, knowing that your labor is not empty in the Lord.

rationale: The advantage of wisdom over folly is pictured as light over darkness; Proverbs contrasts illuminated righteous ways with dark ways that cause stumbling.
source_text: I saw that wisdom has an advantage over folly, like the advantage light has over darkness.

target_units.text: But the ways of the righteous shine like light; they go forward and illuminate until the day comes right.

rationale: The source acknowledges one event for wise and foolish people; the later passage expands the same observation across righteous, ungodly and other contrasting groups.
source_text: The wise person’s eyes are in his head, but the fool walks in darkness. Yet I too knew that one event will happen to them all.

target_units.text: There is futility in everything: one event comes to the righteous and the ungodly, to the good and the bad, to the clean and the unclean, to the one who sacrifices and the one who does not sacrifice. As the good person, so the sinner; as the one who swears, so the one who fears an oath.

rationale: The speaker questions wisdom because he shares the fool's fate; the following verse specifies their shared death and absence of enduring remembrance.
source_text: I said in my heart: The fool’s fate will happen to me too. Why have I been wise? Then I spoke excessively in my heart, because a fool speaks from excess, for this too is futility.

target_units.text: For there is no enduring remembrance of the wise person along with the fool; in the coming days everything will already be forgotten. How will the wise person die along with the fool?

source_text: For there is no enduring remembrance of the wise person along with the fool; in the coming days everything will already be forgotten. How will the wise person die along with the fool?

target_units.text: And he ceased for ever and will live to the end, for he will not see corruption when he sees wise people dying.

source_text: I hated all my toil with which I toil beneath the sun, because I leave it to the person who comes after me.

target_units.text: Will you not leave your labors to another, and your toils to the division of an inheritance?

rationale: The source cannot know the character of the person who will control its toil; the parable asks whose the stored goods will be when their owner dies.
source_text: Who knows whether he will be wise or foolish? Yet he has authority over all the toil with which I labored and acted wisely beneath the sun. This too is futility.

target_units.text: But God said to him, ‘Fool, this very night they demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared—whose will they be?’

rationale: The speaker's withdrawal of heart from toil follows the stated distress that another person, possibly foolish, will control everything produced.

rationale: The source calls it grievous to give one's hard-won portion to someone who did not labor; Sirach similarly anticipates one's labors becoming another's inheritance.
source_text: for a person may toil with wisdom, knowledge and courage, yet will give his portion to someone who did not toil for it. This too is futility and a great evil.

target_units.text: Will you not leave your labors to another, and your toils to the division of an inheritance?

rationale: Both ask what a person obtains from all the toil undertaken beneath the sun, repeating the book's governing question.

target_units.text: What surplus has a person in all his toil at which he toils beneath the sun?

rationale: The source's toiling heart cannot sleep at night; the later contrast says that abundance of riches prevents sleep even while the worker sleeps sweetly.
source_text: For all his days are pain, and his distraction is anger; even at night his heart does not sleep. This too is futility.

target_units.text: Sweet is the slave’s sleep, whether he eats little or much; but being filled with riches does not let him sleep.

rationale: Both explicitly locate eating, drinking and seeing goodness in one's toil in God's giving, rather than treating enjoyment as self-produced.
source_text: There is no good in a person. What he will eat and drink and let his soul see as good in his toil—I saw that this too is from the hand of God.

target_units.text: Moreover, whenever a person eats and drinks and sees good in all his toil, this is God’s gift.

rationale: The question about eating apart from God is developed by the statement that God must empower a person to eat from his possessions.
source_text: For who will eat, and who will abstain, apart from Him?

target_units.text: Moreover, every person to whom God has given wealth and possessions, and whom He has empowered to eat from them, take his portion and rejoice in his toil—this is God’s gift.

source_text: For to the person who is good before Him He gave wisdom, knowledge and gladness; but to the sinner He gave the distraction of adding and gathering, to give to the one who is good before God. This too is futility and resolve of spirit.

target_units.text: behold, I have done according to your word. Behold, I have given you a discerning and wise heart, so that no one like you has been before you, and no one like you shall arise after you.

rationale: The source assigns a time and season to every matter; Daniel explicitly places changes of seasons and times under God's action.

rationale: The source pairs pulling down with building; Jeremiah's commission likewise includes demolishing and building among opposed appointed actions.
source_text: a time to kill and a time to heal, a time to pull down and a time to build,

source_text: a time to tear and a time to sew, a time to be silent and a time to speak,

target_units.text: I set my heart to seek out and examine by wisdom everything that happens beneath heaven, for God gave human beings a grievous distraction to be distracted by.

target_units.text: A person, though in honor, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and made like them.
