rationale: Two can withstand an assailant where one cannot; Sirach describes a faithful friend as a strong shelter, giving a related protective account of friendship.
source_text: If the one gains strength, the two will stand against him; a threefold cord is not quickly torn apart.

target_units.text: A faithful friend is a strong shelter; and whoever has found him has found a treasure.

rationale: The poor wise youth is preferred to the foolish king; Proverbs likewise allows an intelligent servant to rule foolish masters, placing understanding above rank.
source_text: Better a poor and wise youth than an older and foolish king who no longer knows how to pay attention,

target_units.text: An intelligent household servant will rule foolish masters, and divide portions among brothers.

relationship: narrative parallel of elevation from confinement
rationale: The source pictures someone coming from confinement to rule; Joseph is brought from the fortress and, after his discerning counsel, appointed over Egypt. It is a parallel, not an identification.
source_text: for he will come from the prisoners’ house to reign, though he was born poor in his kingdom.

target_units.text: And Pharaoh sent and called Joseph; and they brought him out of the fortress, and shaved him, and changed his garments; and he came to Pharaoh.
And Pharaoh said to Joseph, “I have dreamed a dream, and there is none to interpret it; but I have heard it said concerning you, that when you hear dreams, you can interpret them.”
And Joseph answered Pharaoh, saying, “Without God, no answer bringing deliverance shall be given to Pharaoh.”
And Pharaoh spoke to Joseph, saying, “In my dream I thought I was standing beside the bank of the river.
“And as though from the river there came up seven cows, fair in appearance and choice in flesh, and they grazed among the reeds.
“And behold, seven other cows came up after them from the river, wretched and ugly in appearance and lean in flesh; I have never seen such ugly cows in all the land of Egypt.
“And the seven ugly and lean cows devoured the first seven cows, which were fair and choice.
“And they entered into their bellies, yet it could not be perceived that they had entered into their bellies; and their appearance was ugly as at first. And I awoke, and slept again.
“And I saw again in my dream, and as though seven ears of grain came up upon one stalk, full and good.
“And seven other ears sprouted beside them, thin and blighted by the wind.
“And the seven thin ears, blighted by the wind, swallowed the seven good and full ears. I told the interpreters, but there was none to explain it to me.”
And Joseph said to Pharaoh, “Pharaoh’s dream is one. God has shown to Pharaoh what He is about to do.
“The seven fair cows are seven years, and the seven good ears are seven years. Pharaoh’s dream is one.
“And the seven lean cows which came up after them are seven years; and the seven thin ears, blighted by the wind, shall be seven years of famine.
“And this is the word which I have spoken to Pharaoh: God has shown to Pharaoh what He is about to do.
“Behold, seven years of great abundance are coming in all the land of Egypt.
“And seven years of famine shall come after them, and they shall forget the plenty in all the land of Egypt; and the famine shall consume the land.
“And the abundance shall not be known in the land because of the famine which shall follow, for it shall be exceedingly severe.
“And as for Pharaoh’s dream being repeated twice, it is because the word from God shall be true, and God shall hasten to do it.
“Now therefore seek out a prudent and discerning man, and set him over the land of Egypt.
“And let Pharaoh act, and appoint governors over the land; and let them take a fifth of all the produce of the land of Egypt during the seven years of abundance.
“And let them gather all the food of these seven good years which are coming; and let the grain be gathered under Pharaoh’s hand, and let food be kept in the cities.
“And the food shall be kept for the land against the seven years of famine which shall be in the land of Egypt, and the land shall not be destroyed by the famine.”
And the words pleased Pharaoh and all his servants.
And Pharaoh said to all his servants, “Shall we find such a man as this, who has the Spirit of God in him?”
And Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Since God has shown you all these things, there is no man more prudent and discerning than you.
“You shall be over my house, and all my people shall obey your mouth; only in the throne shall I be above you.”
And Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Behold, I set you today over all the land of Egypt.”

rationale: The source urges approaching God's house to listen while criticizing fools' gifts; Samuel explicitly ranks listening and attentiveness above sacrifice.
source_text: Guard your foot when you go to God’s house, and be near to listen. Your sacrifice is better than the fools’ gift, for they do not know how to do evil.

target_units.text: Samuel said, “Are whole burnt offerings and sacrifices as desirable to the Lord as listening to the Lord’s voice? Behold, obedience is better than sacrifice, and attentiveness than the fat of rams.

rationale: The source calls for few words before God in heaven; Jesus rejects babbling many words and begins the model prayer by addressing the Father in heaven.
source_text: Do not be hasty with your mouth, and do not let your heart hurry to bring out a word before God, for God is in heaven and you are on earth. Therefore let your words be few.

target_units.text: When praying, do not babble like the Gentiles, for they think they will be heard through their many words.
So do not become like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask Him.
Pray, then, in this way: ‘Our Father who art in the heavens, hallowed be Thy name.

rationale: The source associates a fool's voice with many words; Proverbs warns that much talking does not escape sin and commends restraint of the lips.
source_text: For a dream comes with much distraction, and a fool’s voice with many words.

target_units.text: Through much talking you will not escape sin, but by sparing your lips you will be intelligent.

rationale: Both command someone who vows to God not to delay paying the vow; the Deuteronomy passage explicitly makes failure sinful.
source_text: Whenever you vow a vow to God, do not delay paying it, for there is no delight in fools. Pay whatever you vow.

target_units.text: And if you vow a vow unto the Lord your God, you shall not delay to pay it; for the Lord your God shall surely require it of you, and there shall be sin upon you.

rationale: The source prefers abstaining from a vow to failing to pay; Deuteronomy expressly says there is no sin in choosing not to vow.
source_text: Better that you do not vow than that you vow and do not pay.

target_units.text: But if you do not desire to vow, there is no sin upon you.

rationale: The source refuses an excuse of ignorance for a mouth that incurs sin; Deuteronomy requires doing what one's lips have spoken as a gift vowed to God.
source_text: Do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin, and do not say before God, “It was ignorance,” lest God become angry at your voice and destroy the works of your hands.

target_units.text: That which proceeds through your lips you shall keep and do, as you have vowed a gift unto the Lord your God, which you have spoken with your mouth.

rationale: Fear of God answers the source's abundance of futile dreams and words; the same imperative governs the book's concluding summary.
source_text: For with many dreams come futilities and many words; therefore fear God.

target_units.text: The conclusion of the matter—the whole is heard: fear God and keep His commandments, for this is the whole human being.

rationale: The source names extortion of the poor and stolen justice; James depicts withheld laborers' wages together with condemnation and murder of a righteous person.
source_text: If you see extortion of the poor and robbery of judgment and righteousness in a region, do not be astonished at the matter, for a high official is above another to keep watch, and higher ones are above them.

target_units.text: Look, the wages of the laborers who reaped your fields, withheld by you, cry out; and the cries of the harvesters have entered the ears of the Lord Sabaoth.
You lived luxuriously on the earth and indulged yourselves; you fattened your hearts on a day of slaughter.
You condemned; you murdered the righteous one. He does not oppose you.

rationale: The silver lover is never filled with silver; Proverbs likewise presents human eyes as insatiable, describing the appetite that possession does not satisfy.
source_text: Whoever loves silver will not be filled with silver; and who has loved a yield in their abundance? This too is futility.

target_units.text: Hades and destruction are not filled, and likewise human eyes are insatiable.

rationale: Increasing goods leaves their owner merely looking while others consume; the target likewise describes possessions from which a stranger, rather than the owner, eats.
source_text: When goodness increased, those who consumed it multiplied. What strength has its possessor except to look at it with his eyes?

target_units.text: a person to whom God will give wealth, possessions and glory, so that his soul lacks nothing it desires, yet God will not empower him to eat from it, for a stranger will eat it. This is futility and a grievous sickness.

rationale: Riches prevent their owner's sleep in the source; the earlier account of painful toil likewise leaves the heart awake at night.
source_text: Sweet is the slave’s sleep, whether he eats little or much; but being filled with riches does not let him sleep.

target_units.text: For all his days are pain, and his distraction is anger; even at night his heart does not sleep. This too is futility.

rationale: Wealth is kept to its owner's harm; Paul describes the desire for riches and love of money leading people into ruin and many pains.
source_text: There is a sickness I have seen beneath the sun: wealth kept by its possessor to his harm,

target_units.text: But those who want to become rich fall into temptation and a snare and many foolish and harmful desires, which plunge people into ruin and destruction.
For the love of money is a root of all evils, and some, reaching for it, wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many pains.

rationale: The source depicts wealth disappearing and leaving a son empty-handed; Paul's warning against hoping in uncertain wealth states the principle illustrated by that loss.
source_text: and that wealth will be lost through a grievous distraction, and he fathered a son with nothing in his hand.

target_units.text: Command those who are rich in the present age not to be arrogant nor to set their hope on the uncertainty of wealth, but on God, who richly provides us all things for enjoyment,

rationale: Both describe coming naked from the mother's womb and departing naked, using the same birth-and-departure comparison to deny lasting possession.
source_text: As he came naked from his mother’s womb, he will return to depart as he came. He will take nothing from his toil to carry in his hand.

target_units.text: “I myself came out naked from my mother’s womb, and naked I shall depart there: the Lord gave, and the Lord took away; as it seemed good to the Lord, so it happened: blessed be the name of the Lord.”

relationship: parallel inability to carry wealth away
rationale: The source says a person departs as he came despite toil; Paul likewise says people brought nothing into the world and can carry nothing out.
source_text: This too is a grievous sickness: just as he came, so he will depart. What surplus has he from toiling for the wind?

target_units.text: For we brought nothing into the world, because neither can we carry anything out.

rationale: The source's days of darkness, mourning and anger recall the earlier description of all one's days as pain and one's distraction as anger.
source_text: All his days are in darkness and mourning, with much anger, sickness and wrath.

target_units.text: For all his days are pain, and his distraction is anger; even at night his heart does not sleep. This too is futility.

rationale: Both commend eating, drinking and seeing goodness in one's toil within God's provision, giving the same practical response to labor's limits.
source_text: Behold, what I have seen to be good and fitting is to eat and drink and see goodness in all one’s toil beneath the sun during the numbered days of life God has given, for that is one’s portion.

target_units.text: Moreover, whenever a person eats and drinks and sees good in all his toil, this is God’s gift.

rationale: God both grants possessions and enables their enjoyment in the source; Paul directs the wealthy toward God as the provider of things for enjoyment.
source_text: Moreover, every person to whom God has given wealth and possessions, and whom He has empowered to eat from them, take his portion and rejoice in his toil—this is God’s gift.

target_units.text: Command those who are rich in the present age not to be arrogant nor to set their hope on the uncertainty of wealth, but on God, who richly provides us all things for enjoyment,

rationale: God occupies the person's heart with gladness; the later saying describes rejoicing as accompanying a person through the days God gives.
source_text: For he will not often remember the days of his life, because God distracts him with the gladness of his heart.

target_units.text: So I praised gladness, because a person has no good under the sun except to eat, drink and rejoice; this will accompany him in his toil through the days of his life that God gave him under the sun.

relationship: explicit contrast in enjoyment of wealth
rationale: Both describe God-given possessions, but the source denies the owner power to eat while the earlier passage makes that power a further gift from God.
source_text: a person to whom God will give wealth, possessions and glory, so that his soul lacks nothing it desires, yet God will not empower him to eat from it, for a stranger will eat it. This is futility and a grievous sickness.

target_units.text: Moreover, every person to whom God has given wealth and possessions, and whom He has empowered to eat from them, take his portion and rejoice in his toil—this is God’s gift.

relationship: parallel preference for a stillborn condition
rationale: The source prefers a stillborn child to long life without goodness; Job likewise imagines rest through death at birth or the condition of a miscarriage.
source_text: If a man fathers a hundred children and lives many years, however numerous the days of his years, but his soul is not filled with goodness and he has no burial, I said a stillborn child is better off than he,

target_units.text: For why did I not die in the womb, come out from the belly and immediately perish?
Why did knees meet me? Why did I suck breasts?
Now I would have lain down and been quiet; I would have slept and rested
with kings, counselors of the earth, who exulted in swords,
or with rulers who had much gold, who filled their houses with silver,
or like a miscarriage coming out of a mother’s womb, or like infants who never saw light.

rationale: The source's stillborn child has not seen the sun yet has more rest; Job joins imagined rest in death to infants who never saw light.
source_text: and though it has not seen the sun or known anything, it has more rest than he.

target_units.text: Now I would have lain down and been quiet; I would have slept and rested
with kings, counselors of the earth, who exulted in swords,
or with rulers who had much gold, who filled their houses with silver,
or like a miscarriage coming out of a mother’s womb, or like infants who never saw light.

rationale: Even greatly prolonged life ends at the one place in the source; the earlier passage explicitly says all go to one place and return to dust.
source_text: Even if he lived through courses of a thousand years but saw no goodness, do not all go to one place?

target_units.text: All go to one place; all came from dust, and all return to dust.

rationale: The source says labor feeds the mouth without filling appetite; Proverbs similarly characterizes human eyes as insatiable, emphasizing desire's persistence.
source_text: All a person’s toil is for his mouth, yet his appetite will not be filled.

target_units.text: Hades and destruction are not filled, and likewise human eyes are insatiable.

rationale: The question about the wise person's advantage over the fool resumes the earlier tension between wisdom's benefit and the death shared by wise and foolish alike.
source_text: For what advantage has the wise person over the fool? For the poor person knows how to walk before life.

target_units.text: The wise person’s eyes are in his head, but the fool walks in darkness. Yet I too knew that one event will happen to them all.
I said in my heart: The fool’s fate will happen to me too. Why have I been wise? Then I spoke excessively in my heart, because a fool speaks from excess, for this too is futility.
For there is no enduring remembrance of the wise person along with the fool; in the coming days everything will already be forgotten. How will the wise person die along with the fool?

rationale: The source prefers what the eyes actually see to wandering appetite; Paul similarly commends contentment with present food and coverings.
source_text: Better a sight for the eyes than wandering in appetite. This too is futility and resolve of spirit.

target_units.text: But having food and coverings, with these we will be content.

relationship: parallel inability to contend with superior power
rationale: The source denies a human being's ability to contend in judgment with one stronger; Job expressly denies successful litigation or resistance against the mighty Lord.
source_text: Whatever has come to be has already been named, and it is known what a human being is; he will not be able to contend in judgment with one stronger than himself.

target_units.text: For if he wishes to enter judgment with Him, He certainly will not listen to him, lest he answer back to one of His words out of a thousand.
For He is wise in understanding, mighty and great. Who grew hard against Him and endured?

rationale: Many words increase futility in the source; Proverbs warns that much talking fails to escape sin and instead commends restrained lips.
source_text: For many words increase futility; what advantage has a person?

target_units.text: Through much talking you will not escape sin, but by sparing your lips you will be intelligent.

relationship: shared ignorance and brevity of life
rationale: The source asks who knows life's good or future and likens life to a shadow; James combines ignorance of tomorrow with the image of a disappearing vapor.
source_text: For who knows what is good for a person in life, during the numbered days of his life of futility? He has spent them in a shadow. Who will tell a person what will be after him beneath the sun?

target_units.text: you who do not know what tomorrow brings. What is your life? For you are a vapor, appearing for a little while and then disappearing.

relationship: parallel value of a good name
rationale: The source prefers a name to good oil; Proverbs likewise values a good name above great wealth and favor above silver and gold.
source_text: A name is better than good oil, and the day of death than the day of one’s birth.

target_units.text: A good name is more desirable than much wealth, and good favor is above silver and gold.

rationale: The house of mourning makes the living take everyone's end to heart; Sirach similarly instructs remembering one's last things as a guard against sin.
source_text: Better to go to a house of mourning than to a house of drinking, for this is the end of every human being, and the living will take it to heart.

target_units.text: In all your words remember your last things, and you will never sin.

rationale: A troubled face can improve the heart in the source; the psalmist likewise calls humiliation good because it taught him God's ordinances.
source_text: Anger is better than laughter, for through a troubled face the heart will become better.

target_units.text: It is good for me that Thou didst humble me, so that I might learn Thine ordinances.

rationale: The contrast between wise hearts in mourning and fools in gladness rests on the earlier explanation that mourning makes the living take mortality to heart.
source_text: The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, but the heart of fools is in the house of gladness.

target_units.text: Better to go to a house of mourning than to a house of drinking, for this is the end of every human being, and the living will take it to heart.

rationale: The source prefers hearing wise rebuke to fools' singing; Proverbs pictures a wise word fitting a receptive ear like a precious ornament.
source_text: Better to hear a wise person’s rebuke than to be someone listening to the song of fools,

target_units.text: A costly carnelian is fastened into a golden earring—a wise word into a receptive ear.

rationale: The source compares foolish laughter to the sound of thorns beneath a cauldron and calls it futility; the earlier experiment similarly labels laughter delirium and questions gladness.
source_text: for like the sound of thorns beneath a cauldron, so is the laughter of fools. This too is futility.

target_units.text: Of laughter I said, “Delirium!” And to gladness, “What are you doing?”

rationale: Extortion drives the wise astray and destroys their heart in the source; Proverbs likewise says receiving bribes destroys the taker.
source_text: For extortion drives a wise person astray and destroys the heart of his vigor.

target_units.text: One who takes bribes destroys himself, but one who hates taking gifts is saved.

rationale: The source ranks a patient person above someone high in spirit; Proverbs likewise places patience and control of anger above physical and military power.
source_text: The end of words is better than their beginning; a patient person is better than one high in spirit.

target_units.text: A patient man is better than a strong man, and one who controls anger is better than one who captures a city.

rationale: The source forbids haste to anger because anger lodges with fools; James commands slowness to anger because human anger fails to accomplish God's righteousness.
source_text: Do not be hasty in your spirit to become angry, for anger will rest in the bosom of fools.

target_units.text: Know this, my beloved brothers: let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger,
for a man’s anger does not accomplish the righteousness of God.

rationale: Wisdom is good alongside an inheritance in the source; Wisdom of Solomon similarly joins good things and wealth to wisdom while treating her as their guide.
source_text: Wisdom is good with an inheritance, and an advantage to those who behold the sun.

target_units.text: But all good things came to me together with her, and immeasurable wealth was in her hands.
I rejoiced in them all, because wisdom leads them, but I did not know that she was their mother.

rationale: The source compares wisdom's shelter with silver but gives life-giving advantage to wisdom; the target likewise values wisdom above wealth and calls her an unfailing treasure.
source_text: For wisdom in its shade is like the shade of silver, and the advantage of the knowledge of wisdom will give life to its possessor.

target_units.text: I preferred her to scepters and thrones, and reckoned wealth as nothing in comparison with her.
Nor did I compare a priceless stone with her, for all gold in her sight is a little sand, and silver will be reckoned as clay before her.
I loved her more than health and beauty, and chose to have her rather than light, because the radiance that comes from her never sleeps.
But all good things came to me together with her, and immeasurable wealth was in her hands.
I rejoiced in them all, because wisdom leads them, but I did not know that she was their mother.
I learned without deceit and share without envy; I do not conceal her wealth.
For she is an unfailing treasure for human beings; those who acquire it enter into friendship with God, commended by the gifts that come from discipline.

rationale: The source asks who can put in order what God has twisted; the earlier proverb similarly states that what is twisted cannot be put in order.
source_text: Consider God’s works, for who can put in order the one whom God has twisted?

target_units.text: What is twisted cannot be put in order, and what is lacking cannot be counted.

rationale: God makes differing days while concealing what comes afterward in the source; the earlier passage joins God's fitting ordering of times to humanity's inability to discover His whole work.
source_text: On a day of goodness, live in good; on a day of evil, consider: God has made this in accord with that concerning speech, so that human beings may find out nothing that comes after them.

target_units.text: He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also put the age in their hearts, so that human beings may not find out the work God has done from beginning to end.

rationale: The source observes righteousness ending in death while evil continues; the psalm likewise juxtaposes prospering sinners with the righteous speaker's persistent affliction.
source_text: I have seen everything in my days of futility: a righteous person perishing in his righteousness, and an ungodly person remaining in his evil.

target_units.text: Behold, these are sinners, and they prosper; for the age they took possession of wealth.
And I said, “Then in vain I made my heart righteous and washed my hands among the innocent;
and I became scourged all day, and my rebuke comes in the mornings.”

rationale: The source's warning against being excessively wise is compared with Sirach's prohibition on investigating beyond human strength; this addresses the wisdom clause without equating righteousness with sin.
source_text: Do not become overly righteous, and do not be excessively wise, lest you be bewildered.

target_units.text: Do not seek things too difficult for you, and do not investigate things beyond your strength.
Consider the things commanded you, for you have no need of hidden things.
Do not busy yourself with matters beyond your tasks, for more than human understanding has been shown to you.
For their assumption has misled many, and an evil suspicion has caused their thoughts to slip.

relationship: parallel warning about ungodliness and lifespan
rationale: The source warns that great ungodliness may bring death before one's time; the later saying denies the ungodly lasting good and prolonged days.
source_text: Do not be greatly ungodly, and do not become harsh, lest you die before your time.

target_units.text: But it will not be good for the ungodly, and he will not prolong his days in a shadow, because he does not fear before God.

rationale: Holding to both warnings refers to the preceding cautions against excessive righteousness or wisdom and great ungodliness; fearing God supplies the stated way through both dangers.
source_text: It is good for you to hold to this and also not release your hand from that, for the one who fears God will come through them all.

target_units.text: Do not become overly righteous, and do not be excessively wise, lest you be bewildered.
Do not be greatly ungodly, and do not become harsh, lest you die before your time.

relationship: parallel superiority of wisdom to force
rationale: Wisdom helps more than ten city rulers in the source; Proverbs prefers wisdom to strength and associates successful warfare with deliberation.
source_text: Wisdom will help the wise person more than ten rulers who are in the city,

target_units.text: A wise person is better than a strong one, and a man with understanding than a great cultivated estate;
with steering war takes place, and help is with a deliberative heart.

rationale: The source denies an earthly righteous person who never sins; Paul likewise charges all with sin and cites the absence of even one righteous person.
source_text: for there is no righteous person on earth who will do good and not sin.

target_units.text: What, then? Are we better off? Not at all; for we have already charged both Jews and Greeks with all being under sin,
just as it is written: “There is no righteous one, not even one;
there is no one who understands; there is no one who seeks God.
All turned aside; together they became useless. There is no one who shows kindness; there is not even one.

rationale: The instruction not to attend to every spoken insult is grounded in the following reminder that the hearer has also cursed others.
source_text: Also, do not set your heart upon every word people speak, so that you may not hear your slave cursing you,

target_units.text: for very often he will wrong you, and many times he will hurt your heart, just as you too have cursed others.

rationale: The source recalls one's own curses when hurt by another's speech; Jesus likewise requires attention to one's own fault before correcting another's.
source_text: for very often he will wrong you, and many times he will hurt your heart, just as you too have cursed others.

target_units.text: Why do you see the splinter in your brother’s eye, but do not notice the beam in your own eye?
Or how will you say to your brother, ‘Let me remove the splinter from your eye,’ when behold, the beam is in your own eye?
Hypocrite! First remove the beam from your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the splinter from your brother’s eye.

rationale: The resolve to become wise and test matters by wisdom resumes the earlier determination to know wisdom and understanding.
source_text: All this I tested by wisdom. I said, “I will be wise,”

target_units.text: I set my heart to know wisdom and knowledge; I came to know comparisons and understanding, for this too is resolve of spirit.

rationale: Wisdom has withdrawn into an unfathomable depth in the source; Job asks where wisdom can be found and has the abyss deny possessing it.
source_text: but it moved far away from me, farther than it was; and depth is deep—who can find it?

target_units.text: But where was wisdom found, and what is the place of knowledge?
A mortal does not know its way, and it will certainly not be found among humans.
The abyss said, ‘It is not in me,’ and the sea said, ‘It is not with me.’

rationale: The source continues the earlier intentional pursuit of wisdom and knowledge, now explicitly extending its inquiry to an ungodly person's folly, harshness and delirium.
source_text: I turned, I and my heart, to know, examine and seek wisdom and a reckoning, and to know an ungodly person’s folly, harshness and delirium.

target_units.text: I set my heart to know wisdom and knowledge; I came to know comparisons and understanding, for this too is resolve of spirit.

rationale: The source depicts a woman as nets and bonds catching the sinner; Proverbs depicts seductive speech as snares leading the victim toward slaughter and Hades.
source_text: I find more bitter than death the woman who is traps, whose heart is nets and whose hands are bonds. The one who is good before God will be rescued from her, but the sinner will be caught by her.

target_units.text: She led him astray with much conversation and drove him off course with snares from her lips.
He followed her, made a fool, as an ox is led to slaughter and as a dog to bonds,
or as a deer struck in the liver by an arrow. He hurries like a bird into a trap, not knowing that he runs for his life.
Now therefore, son, listen to me, and attend to my mouth’s sayings.
Do not let your heart turn aside to her ways.
For she has wounded and brought down many, and those she has murdered are beyond counting.
Her house is ways to Hades, leading down to death’s chambers.

rationale: The source distinguishes God's upright creation of humanity from later human reasonings; Genesis depicts male and female humanity within the creation God judges very good.
source_text: Only behold, this I found: God made humankind upright, but they sought many reasonings.

target_units.text: And God made man; in the image of God He made him; male and female He made them.

And God blessed them, saying, “Grow and multiply, and fill the earth and subdue it. Rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, all the cattle, all the earth, and every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth.”
And God said, “Behold, I have given you every plant sowing seed upon all the earth, and every tree that bears fruit containing seed. These shall be yours for food.
And to every wild beast of the earth, every bird of heaven, and every creeping thing upon the earth that has life within it, I have given every green plant for food.” And it was so.
And God saw all that He had made, and behold, it was very good. And there was evening, and there was morning: a sixth day.

rationale: The source asks who knows the solution of a saying; Proverbs describes discerning people learning to understand obscure sayings and riddles.
source_text: Who knows wise people, and who knows the solution of a saying? A person’s wisdom will light up his face, but one with a shameless face will be hated.

target_units.text: For a wise person who hears these things will become wiser, and the discerning will acquire guidance,
and understand a comparison and an obscure saying, the utterances of the wise and riddles.

relationship: related care over words sworn to God
rationale: The source warns against haste concerning an oath of God; the earlier instructions require payment of vows and refuse excuses for rashly spoken obligations.
source_text: Guard the king’s mouth; and concerning the word of an oath of God, do not hurry.

target_units.text: Whenever you vow a vow to God, do not delay paying it, for there is no delight in fools. Pay whatever you vow.
Better that you do not vow than that you vow and do not pay.
Do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin, and do not say before God, “It was ignorance,” lest God become angry at your voice and destroy the works of your hands.

rationale: The warning about standing in an evil matter is followed by the explanation that a king speaks with authority and resists questioning, clarifying the practical danger.
source_text: You will go from his presence. Do not stand in an evil matter, for he will do whatever he pleases,

target_units.text: just as a king with authority speaks; and who will say to him, “What will you do?”

relationship: contrast between royal and divine authority
rationale: The source presents the king's word as difficult to challenge; Daniel places kings beneath God, who transfers and appoints them, qualifying that earthly authority.
source_text: just as a king with authority speaks; and who will say to him, “What will you do?”

target_units.text: He changes seasons and times, transfers kings and appoints them, gives wisdom to the wise and understanding to those who possess knowledge,

rationale: The wise heart knows a time of judgment; the earlier passage likewise joins God's judgment of righteous and ungodly people to a time for every work.
source_text: Whoever keeps a command will know no evil word, and a wise heart knows a time of judgment.

target_units.text: I said in my heart: God will judge the righteous and the ungodly, for there is a time for every matter and for every work.

rationale: The source's assertion that every matter has a time and judgment repeats the earlier premise that every matter beneath heaven has its season.
source_text: For every matter has a time and judgment, because a person’s knowledge is great upon him.

target_units.text: For all things there is a time, and a season for every matter beneath heaven.

rationale: Both say a person does not know what will follow and ask who can tell him, restating the limit on human foresight.
source_text: For he does not know what will be; who will tell him how it will be?

target_units.text: For who knows what is good for a person in life, during the numbered days of his life of futility? He has spent them in a shadow. Who will tell a person what will be after him beneath the sun?

rationale: No one controls the day of death in the source; Hebrews likewise treats dying as an appointment for human beings and places judgment after it.
source_text: No human being has authority over the spirit to restrain the spirit, and there is no authority over the day of death. There is no discharge in war, and ungodliness will not rescue the one who possesses it.

target_units.text: And just as it is appointed for people to die once, and after this judgment,

rationale: The source explicitly sees one person's authority harming another; the earlier scene depicts power in oppressors' hands and tears among those without comfort.
source_text: All this I saw, and I set my heart upon every deed done under the sun, all the things in which one person had authority over another to his harm.

target_units.text: Again I turned and saw all the extortions committed beneath the sun. Behold, the tears of those being extorted, with no one to comfort them! Power was in their extorters’ hands, and they had no one to comfort them.

rationale: Public praise for the ungodly anticipates the later complaint that ungodly people receive outcomes appropriate to righteous deeds.
source_text: Then I saw ungodly people brought into tombs; they went from the holy place and were praised in the city because they had acted so. This too is futility.

target_units.text: There is a futility that occurs on earth: there are righteous people to whom things happen as the deeds of the ungodly deserve, and ungodly people to whom things happen as the deeds of the righteous deserve. I said that this too is futility.

rationale: The source describes people emboldened in evil when no prompt opposition comes; Paul warns that despising divine forbearance stores up future wrath rather than granting impunity.
source_text: Because no prompt contradiction comes from those who do evil, the heart of human beings therefore became fully assured in them to do evil.

target_units.text: Or do you despise the wealth of His kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God’s kindness leads you to repentance?
But by your hardness and unrepentant heart, you store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and revelation of God’s righteous judgment,

rationale: The sinner's apparent length of days is balanced by assurance for those who fear God; the following verse denies lasting good to the ungodly who lack that fear.
source_text: The sinner has done evil from then, and there is length for him; for I know that it will be good for those who fear God, so that they may fear before Him.

target_units.text: But it will not be good for the ungodly, and he will not prolong his days in a shadow, because he does not fear before God.

rationale: The source denies lasting good and prolonged days to the ungodly; the psalm portrays an exalted ungodly person vanishing and contrasts him with the peaceful person's remnant.
source_text: But it will not be good for the ungodly, and he will not prolong his days in a shadow, because he does not fear before God.

target_units.text: I saw an ungodly person raised high and lifting himself like the cedars of Lebanon.
I passed by, and behold, he was gone; I sought him, but his place could not be found.
Guard innocence and look upon uprightness, for a peaceful person has a remnant.
But the lawless will be destroyed together; the remnants of the ungodly will be destroyed.

rationale: The source complains that righteous and ungodly people receive each other's expected outcomes; the psalm contrasts thriving sinners with the righteous speaker's daily affliction.
source_text: There is a futility that occurs on earth: there are righteous people to whom things happen as the deeds of the ungodly deserve, and ungodly people to whom things happen as the deeds of the righteous deserve. I said that this too is futility.

target_units.text: Behold, these are sinners, and they prosper; for the age they took possession of wealth.
And I said, “Then in vain I made my heart righteous and washed my hands among the innocent;
and I became scourged all day, and my rebuke comes in the mornings.”

rationale: Both commend eating, drinking and rejoicing amid toil through the limited days God has given beneath the sun.
source_text: So I praised gladness, because a person has no good under the sun except to eat, drink and rejoice; this will accompany him in his toil through the days of his life that God gave him under the sun.

target_units.text: Behold, what I have seen to be good and fitting is to eat and drink and see goodness in all one’s toil beneath the sun during the numbered days of life God has given, for that is one’s portion.

rationale: The speaker again sets his heart to know wisdom and inspect earthly distraction, resuming the inquiry first announced over everything beneath heaven.
source_text: When I set my heart to know wisdom and to see the distraction carried on upon the earth, because neither by day nor by night does one see sleep with one’s eyes,

target_units.text: I set my heart to seek out and examine by wisdom everything that happens beneath heaven, for God gave human beings a grievous distraction to be distracted by.

relationship: repeated inability to discover God's work
rationale: Both explicitly deny human access to the whole of God's work; the source intensifies this by including the wise person's unsuccessful searching.
source_text: then I saw all God’s works: a person cannot find the work done under the sun. However much a person toils to seek it, he will not find it; even if the wise person says he knows, he will not be able to find it.

target_units.text: He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also put the age in their hearts, so that human beings may not find out the work God has done from beginning to end.

rationale: Both place the righteous in God's hand; Wisdom of Solomon develops that image into peace and hope of immortality despite appearances of death.
source_text: For I set all this upon my heart, and my heart saw all this: the righteous, the wise and their works are in God’s hand. A person knows neither love nor hatred; everything lies before them.

target_units.text: But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and torment will surely not touch them.
In the eyes of the foolish they seemed to have died, and their departure was reckoned a calamity,
and their going away from us a destruction; but they are in peace.
For even if they are punished in the sight of human beings, their hope is full of immortality;

rationale: One event comes to all the source's morally and ritually distinct groups; the earlier passage makes the same observation about wise and foolish people.
source_text: There is futility in everything: one event comes to the righteous and the ungodly, to the good and the bad, to the clean and the unclean, to the one who sacrifices and the one who does not sacrifice. As the good person, so the sinner; as the one who swears, so the one who fears an oath.

target_units.text: The wise person’s eyes are in his head, but the fool walks in darkness. Yet I too knew that one event will happen to them all.

relationship: parallel pervasive evil of the heart
rationale: The source describes human hearts as full of evil during life; Genesis likewise describes continual human inclination of the heart toward evil.
source_text: This is an evil in all that is done under the sun: one event comes to everyone. Moreover, the heart of human beings is full of evil, and delirium is in their heart during their lives; afterward they go to the dead.

target_units.text: And the Lord God saw that the wickedness of mankind had multiplied upon the earth, and that each one continually set his heart upon evil all his days.

rationale: The living person's hope, illustrated by a living dog over a dead lion, is followed by the contrast between living awareness and the dead's lost knowledge and reward.
source_text: Who shares with all the living? There is hope, for a living dog is better than a dead lion.

target_units.text: For the living will know that they will die, but the dead know nothing; they have no further reward, for their memory is forgotten.

relationship: parallel cessation of thought at death
rationale: The source says the dead know nothing and lose remembrance; the psalm likewise describes a departing spirit and the perishing of the person's reasonings that day.
source_text: For the living will know that they will die, but the dead know nothing; they have no further reward, for their memory is forgotten.

target_units.text: His spirit will go out, and he will return to his earth; on that day all their reasonings will perish.

relationship: same-chapter limit on participation after death
rationale: The dead lose their share in earthly activity in the source; the later exhortation grounds present action in the absence of deed, knowledge and wisdom in Hades.
source_text: Their love, their hatred and their envy have already perished; they have no further share for ever in anything done under the sun.

target_units.text: Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your strength, for there is no deed, reckoning, knowledge or wisdom in Hades, where you are going.

relationship: repeated joyful eating under divine favor
rationale: The source commends glad eating and drinking under God's favor; the earlier passage calls eating, drinking and seeing good in toil God's gift.
source_text: Come, eat your bread with gladness and drink your wine with a good heart, for God has already favored your deeds.

target_units.text: Moreover, whenever a person eats and drinks and sees good in all his toil, this is God’s gift.

rationale: The source urges enjoying life with the woman one loves; Proverbs likewise commands shared joy and continuing affectionate companionship with one's own wife.
source_text: Enjoy life with the woman whom you have loved, all the days of your futile life that have been given you under the sun, all your futile days; for this is your share in life and in your toil at which you toil under the sun.

target_units.text: Let your fountain of water be your own, and share joy with the wife of your youth.

Let a deer of affection and a colt of your graces keep company with you. Let your own woman lead you and be with you at every time, for as you move in the company of her affection, you will be one among many.

rationale: The source commands energetic work before the inactivity of Hades; Jesus likewise urges doing the sender's works while it is day, before night prevents work.
source_text: Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your strength, for there is no deed, reckoning, knowledge or wisdom in Hades, where you are going.

target_units.text: We must work the works of the One who sent Me while it is day. Night is coming, when no one can work.

rationale: The source denies that might guarantees victory; the psalm likewise denies salvation through an army's size, a giant's strength or a horse's power.
source_text: Again I saw under the sun that the race is not to the swift, nor battle to the mighty, nor bread to the wise, nor wealth to those with understanding, nor favor to those with knowledge; for time and encounter will happen to them all.

target_units.text: A king is not saved through a great force, and a giant will not be saved by the abundance of his strength.
A horse is false for salvation, and by the abundance of its power it will not be saved.

rationale: The source pictures an unexpected evil time trapping people suddenly; the rich fool is abruptly told that his soul is demanded that very night.
source_text: For a person does not know his time: like fish caught in an evil net, and birds caught in a snare, so human beings are trapped at an evil time when it falls upon them suddenly.

target_units.text: But God said to him, ‘Fool, this very night they demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared—whose will they be?’

relationship: narrative parallel of a besieged city
rationale: The source describes siegeworks raised against a small city; Samuel likewise records a siege mound and an army preparing to breach a city's wall.
source_text: There was a small city with few people in it; a great king might come against it, surround it and build great siegeworks against it,

target_units.text: They came and besieged him at Abel and Beth-maacah. They heaped up a siege mound against the city, and it stood at the outer defence. All the people with Joab were planning to bring down the wall.

relationship: narrative parallel of wisdom delivering a city
rationale: A poor wise man saves the source's city; in Samuel a wise woman's negotiation ends the siege. The comparison concerns civic rescue through wisdom, not identical actors or outcomes of remembrance.
source_text: and he might find in it a poor wise man, who will deliver the city by his wisdom; yet no one remembered that poor man.

target_units.text: A wise woman called from the wall, “Listen, listen! Please tell Joab to come near here, and I will speak to him.”
He came near her. The woman asked, “Are you Joab?” He said, “I am.” She said to him, “Hear your handmaid’s words.” Joab said, “I am listening.”

She said, “Formerly they spoke a saying: ‘Inquiry was made at Abel and Dan whether the things Israel’s faithful had established had come to an end. They will certainly inquire at Abel, and thus whether they had come to an end.’
I am the peaceable part of Israel’s strongholds. You seek to kill a city and a mother city in Israel. Why drown the Lord’s inheritance?”
Joab answered, “Far be it from me, far be it from me to drown or destroy!

That is not the matter. A man from the hill country of Ephraim, named Sheba son of Bichri, has raised his hand against King David. Give him alone to me, and I will withdraw from the city.” The woman said to Joab, “His head will be thrown to you through the wall.”

The woman went to all the people and spoke to the whole city in her wisdom. She cut off Sheba son of Bichri’s head and threw it to Joab. He sounded the horn, and they dispersed from the city, each to his tents. Joab returned to the king in Jerusalem.

relationship: parallel superiority of wisdom to strength
rationale: The source explicitly prefers wisdom to strength, though the poor wise person is despised; Proverbs similarly calls a wise person better than a strong one.
source_text: I said, Wisdom is better than strength; yet the poor man’s wisdom is despised, and his words are not heard.

target_units.text: A wise person is better than a strong one, and a man with understanding than a great cultivated estate;

rationale: After noting that a poor wise person's words go unheard, the source values quietly heard wisdom above rulers' shouting, correcting the preference for social power over counsel.
source_text: The words of the wise, heard quietly, are better than the shouting of rulers in follies.

target_units.text: I said, Wisdom is better than strength; yet the poor man’s wisdom is despised, and his words are not heard.

rationale: Wisdom is better than weapons of war in the source; Proverbs illustrates that advantage through a wise person bringing down an impious stronghold.
source_text: Wisdom is better than weapons of war, but one sinner will destroy much good.

target_units.text: A wise person mounted fortified cities, and brought down the stronghold in which the impious trusted.

rationale: Death-bringing flies spoil fragrant oil in the source; the preceding chapter likewise says one sinner destroys much good. The comparison concerns the damage image, not a reversal of the source's praise of little wisdom.
source_text: Death-bringing flies will spoil a preparation of fragrant oil; a little wisdom is precious beyond the glory of great folly.

target_units.text: Wisdom is better than weapons of war, but one sinner will destroy much good.

rationale: Right and left distinguish wise and foolish hearts in the source; Proverbs likewise distinguishes good and evil ways through contrasting light and darkness.
source_text: A wise person’s heart is toward his right, but a fool’s heart is toward his left.

target_units.text: But the ways of the righteous shine like light; they go forward and illuminate until the day comes right.
But the ways of the ungodly are dark; they do not know how they stumble.

rationale: The fool's road-going and considerations expose his lack of heart; Proverbs likewise describes the person lacking understanding as led by foolishness instead of wisdom.
source_text: Even when the fool walks along the road, his heart will be lacking, and everything he considers is folly.

target_units.text: One lacking understanding has no use for wisdom, for he is led rather by foolishness.

rationale: The source counsels steadiness and healing when an authority's spirit rises; Proverbs similarly says a yielding answer turns away wrath.
source_text: If the spirit of one in authority rises against you, do not leave your place, for healing will put great sins to rest.

target_units.text: Anger destroys even intelligent people; but a yielding answer turns away wrath, and a painful word stirs up anger.

rationale: The source calls the elevation of a fool an evil; Proverbs likewise says luxury does not benefit a fool and criticizes a servant's insolent rule.
source_text: the fool was set in great heights, while the rich will sit in a low place.

target_units.text: Luxury does not benefit a fool, nor does it benefit a household servant if he begins to rule with insolence.

relationship: contrast in reversal of social rank
rationale: The source places mounted slaves above walking rulers within a complaint about misrule; Proverbs gives a contrasting, wisdom-based reason for a servant to rule foolish masters.
source_text: I saw slaves on horses and rulers walking like slaves upon the ground.

target_units.text: An intelligent household servant will rule foolish masters, and divide portions among brothers.

rationale: Both say that the one who digs a pit falls into it; Proverbs explicitly frames the pit as intended for a neighbor and adds a rebounding stone.
source_text: Whoever digs a pit will fall into it, and whoever tears down a fence will be bitten by a snake.

target_units.text: One who digs a pit for his neighbor will fall into it, and one who rolls a stone rolls it upon himself.

relationship: repeated advantage of wisdom over force
rationale: After a difficulty involving iron and strengthening forces, the source identifies wisdom as the courageous person's advantage; the earlier saying directly prefers wisdom to strength.
source_text: If the iron falls out and he has troubled the face, he will strengthen his forces; and wisdom is the advantage of the courageous man.

target_units.text: I said, Wisdom is better than strength; yet the poor man’s wisdom is despised, and his words are not heard.

rationale: The source says a fool's lips drown him; Proverbs likewise calls the fool's mouth his ruin and his lips a trap for his life.
source_text: The words of a wise person’s mouth are gracious, but a fool’s lips will drown him.

target_units.text: A fool’s mouth is ruin for him, and his lips are a trap for his life.

rationale: Speech moving from folly to evil wandering explains the preceding statement that the fool's own lips bring him down.
source_text: The beginning of his mouth’s words is folly, and the end of his speech is evil wandering.

target_units.text: The words of a wise person’s mouth are gracious, but a fool’s lips will drown him.

rationale: The fool multiplies words despite ignorance of what follows; the earlier passage likewise joins many futile words to the question of who can disclose the future.
source_text: The fool multiplies words. A person did not know what happened, and who will tell him what will be after him?

target_units.text: For many words increase futility; what advantage has a person?
For who knows what is good for a person in life, during the numbered days of his life of futility? He has spent them in a shadow. Who will tell a person what will be after him beneath the sun?

rationale: The fool unable to find the city recalls the earlier fool walking along the road without understanding, giving practical form to the chapter's portrayal of folly.
source_text: The toil of fools will weary them, the one who did not know how to go to the city.

target_units.text: Even when the fool walks along the road, his heart will be lacking, and everything he considers is folly.

rationale: The woe against a young king and rulers feasting in the morning is answered by blessing a land with a freeborn king and rulers who eat at the proper time.
source_text: Woe to you, city, whose king is young and whose rulers eat in the morning!

target_units.text: Blessed are you, land, whose king is a son of free people and whose rulers will eat at the proper time in strength and will not be ashamed!

rationale: The source blesses a land with disciplined rulers; Proverbs likewise credits a righteous king with raising up a country, in contrast to lawless destruction.
source_text: Blessed are you, land, whose king is a son of free people and whose rulers will eat at the proper time in strength and will not be ashamed!

target_units.text: A righteous king raises up a country, but a lawless man tears it down.

rationale: Idle hands allow a house to leak and its roof to sink; Proverbs likewise connects prolonged inactivity with the arrival of poverty and want.
source_text: Through laziness the roof beams will sink, and through idle hands the house will leak.

target_units.text: How long will you remain lying down, sluggard? When will you rise from sleep?
You sleep a little, sit a little, doze a little, and clasp your chest with your hands a little;
then poverty arrives beside you like an evil traveler, and want like a good runner.

relationship: shared disclosure principle in different settings
rationale: The source warns that even private curses may be reported; Jesus likewise says hidden things will become known, though His setting concerns fearless witness rather than courtly caution.
source_text: Even in your conscience do not curse a king, and in the inner rooms of your bedchambers do not curse a rich person, for a bird of the heavens will carry the sound, and one with wings will report the word.

target_units.text: So do not fear them. For nothing is covered that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not become known.

rationale: Bread sent upon water is found after many days; Jesus likewise depicts giving as followed by return. This comparison does not settle whether the source pictures commerce or generosity.
source_text: Send forth your bread upon the face of the water, for after many days you will find it.

target_units.text: Give, and it will be given to you. They will put into your lap a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, overflowing; for by the measure you measure, it will be measured back to you.”

rationale: Sharing among seven and eight is urged because future evil is unknown; sowing morning and evening similarly spreads effort because the successful outcome is unknown.
source_text: Give a share to seven, and also to eight, for you do not know what evil will occur upon the earth.

target_units.text: In the morning sow your seed, and toward evening do not let your hand rest, for you do not know which will proceed, this or that, or whether both together will be good.

rationale: Watching uncertain weather prevents sowing and reaping; the later command instead urges repeated sowing despite not knowing which effort will succeed.
source_text: Whoever watches the wind will not sow, and whoever looks at the clouds will not reap,

target_units.text: In the morning sow your seed, and toward evening do not let your hand rest, for you do not know which will proceed, this or that, or whether both together will be good.

relationship: shared hidden formation in the womb
rationale: The source compares unknowable divine work to bones in a pregnant womb; the psalm describes God knowing and forming hidden bones and unworked substance before birth.
source_text: among which no one knows the way of the spirit. As with bones in the womb of the pregnant woman, so you will not know God’s works, all that He will make.

target_units.text: For Thou didst acquire my kidneys, Lord; Thou didst support me from my mother’s womb.
I will thank Thee, for I was made fearfully wonderful; wondrous are Thy works, and my soul knows very well.
My bone was not hidden from Thee, which Thou madest in secret, and my substance in earth’s lowest places.
Thine eyes saw my unworked substance, and in Thy book all will be written; they will be formed over days, and none among them.

rationale: The source urges continued sowing because success is uncertain; Paul likewise urges perseverance but promises a harvest for doing good without giving up.
source_text: In the morning sow your seed, and toward evening do not let your hand rest, for you do not know which will proceed, this or that, or whether both together will be good.

target_units.text: And let us not grow weary in doing good, for in the proper season we will reap, if we do not give up.

relationship: literary contrast of light and decline
rationale: The sweetness of light and seeing the sun contrasts with the approaching darkening of sun, light, moon and stars in the closing portrayal of decline.
source_text: Light is sweet, and it is good for the eyes to see the sun.

target_units.text: before the sun, the light, the moon and the stars grow dark, and the clouds return after the rain;

relationship: progression from enjoyment to difficult years
rationale: The source joins rejoicing over many years with remembering dark days; the following chapter anticipates years in which the aging person has no desire.
source_text: For even if a person lives many years, he will rejoice in them all and remember the days of darkness, for they will be many. All that comes is futility.

target_units.text: Remember the One who created you in the days of your youth, before the days of evil come and the years arrive in which you will say, “I have no desire in them”;

rationale: The source bounds youthful enjoyment with God's coming judgment; the conclusion repeats that every deed, good or evil, enters that judgment.
source_text: Rejoice, young man, in your youth, and let your heart make you glad in the days of your youth. Walk in the ways of your heart and in the sight of your eyes, and know that for all these God will bring you into judgment.

target_units.text: For God will bring every deed into judgment, concerning everything overlooked, whether good or evil.

relationship: parallel removal of anger and evil
rationale: The source commands removing anger and putting away evil; James similarly combines slowness to anger with putting away impurity and abundant evil.
source_text: Remove anger from your heart and put away evil from your flesh, for youth and lack of understanding are futility.

target_units.text: Know this, my beloved brothers: let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger,
for a man’s anger does not accomplish the righteousness of God.
Therefore, putting away every impurity and the abundance of evil, receive with gentleness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls.

rationale: Remembering the Creator during youth complements the preceding invitation to youthful gladness that is explicitly bounded by awareness of God's judgment.
source_text: Remember the One who created you in the days of your youth, before the days of evil come and the years arrive in which you will say, “I have no desire in them”;

target_units.text: Rejoice, young man, in your youth, and let your heart make you glad in the days of your youth. Walk in the ways of your heart and in the sight of your eyes, and know that for all these God will bring you into judgment.

rationale: The darkening heavenly lights reverse the earlier delight in light and seeing the sun, forming a contrast between present vitality and coming decline.
source_text: before the sun, the light, the moon and the stars grow dark, and the clouds return after the rain;

target_units.text: Light is sweet, and it is good for the eyes to see the sun.

relationship: comparison of decline with a contrasting hope
rationale: Shaken keepers, bent strength and failing sight portray decline within the source's mortality poem; Paul acknowledges the outer person's wasting while adding inward renewal. No exact bodily decoding of each image is claimed.
source_text: on the day when the keepers of the house are shaken and the men of strength are bent, when the grinding women have ceased because they have become few and the women looking through the openings grow dark;

target_units.text: Therefore we do not lose heart; but even if our outer person is wasting away, our inner person is being renewed day by day.

rationale: The source sends the human being to an everlasting home amid mourners; the psalm explicitly describes tombs as people's houses for ever.
source_text: when they look from a height and terrors are on the road, when the almond blossoms, the locust grows fat and the caperberry is scattered; for the human being went to his everlasting home, and mourners circled in the marketplace;

target_units.text: Their tombs are their houses for ever, their dwellings from generation to generation; they invoked their names upon their lands.

rationale: Broken vessels and disrupted mechanisms lead into the following declaration of dust returning to earth and spirit to God, placing the images within mortality without assigning them specific organs.
source_text: before the silver cord is overturned, the golden flower ornament is crushed, the jar is broken at the spring and the wheel runs together at the pit;

target_units.text: and the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it.

relationship: reversal of creation's dust and breath
rationale: The source returns dust to earth and spirit to its giver; Genesis describes God forming the human from earth's dust and imparting life's breath.
source_text: and the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it.

target_units.text: And God formed man from the dust of the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life; and man became a living soul.

rationale: The concluding futility declaration repeats the opening formula and its attribution to Ecclesiastes, closing the book's principal frame.
source_text: Futility of futilities, said Ecclesiastes; everything is futility.

target_units.text: Futility of futilities, said Ecclesiastes; futility of futilities, everything is futility.

rationale: Ecclesiastes teaches knowledge, and the unit mentions an orderly arrangement of proverbs; Proverbs similarly introduces a collection intended to teach wisdom, understanding and interpretation of sayings.
source_text: Besides becoming wise, Ecclesiastes also taught the people knowledge; and an ear will trace out an orderly arrangement of proverbs.

target_units.text: The proverbs of Solomon son of David, who reigned in Israel,
for knowing wisdom and discipline and understanding words of good sense,
for receiving turns of speech, understanding true righteousness, and directing judgment rightly,
so that he may give shrewdness to the innocent, perception and thought to a young child.
For a wise person who hears these things will become wiser, and the discerning will acquire guidance,

rationale: The search for delightful and upright words compares with Proverbs' precious-ornament image for spoken speech; the comparison concerns valued expression, not identical claims about truth.
source_text: Ecclesiastes sought much to find words of delight and something written in uprightness, words of truth.

target_units.text: A golden apple on a carnelian necklace—so is speaking a word.

relationship: shared fastening imagery for wise speech
rationale: Wise words are planted nails in the source; Proverbs pictures a wise word fitting a receptive ear as a precious stone fastened in a golden earring.
source_text: The words of the wise are like goads and like planted nails, which were given from collections, from one shepherd, and something beyond them.

target_units.text: A costly carnelian is fastened into a golden earring—a wise word into a receptive ear.

rationale: The warning that much study wearies the flesh recalls the opening observation that increasing knowledge increases pain.
source_text: My son, beware of making many books; there is no limit, and much study is weariness of the flesh.

target_units.text: For in much wisdom is much knowledge, and whoever increases knowledge will increase pain.

rationale: The source summarizes human duty as fearing God and keeping His commandments; Deuteronomy likewise describes God's requirement through fear, service and commandment-keeping.
source_text: The conclusion of the matter—the whole is heard: fear God and keep His commandments, for this is the whole human being.

target_units.text: And now, O Israel, what does the Lord your God require of you, but to fear the Lord your God, to walk in all His ways, and to love Him, and to serve the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul,
to keep the commandments of the Lord your God, and His ordinances which I command you this day, that it may be well with you?

relationship: parallel judgment of good and evil deeds
rationale: Both bring human deeds, whether good or evil, into comprehensive divine judgment; Paul identifies the judgment seat as Christ's.
source_text: For God will bring every deed into judgment, concerning everything overlooked, whether good or evil.

target_units.text: For we must all be revealed before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what is due for what he has done through the body, whether good or evil.
